newsitem.title: USA: Hamas leader says deal will take him to Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Hamas leader says deal will take him to Jordan.

text.p: The jailed leader of the political wing of the Palestinian group Hamas said on Thursday he believed a deal had been struck to send him to Jordan after Israel dropped its extradition bid.

Mousa Mohammed Abu Marzook, a long-time resident of the United States, told Reuters in an interview in the New York prison where he has been held without charge or trial since July 1995 that the Israeli government's announcement on Thursday had not surprised him.

"I knew they would never extradite me," said the soft-spoken Abu Marzook, who was arrested at John F. Kennedy airport after immigration officials found his name on the U.S. list of people with suspected ties to terrorism. "There is no reason to support their accusations, these are unfounded charges against me."

Abu Marzook gave up his appeal against the extradition in January. Israel said on Thursday it was suspending its 18-month-old request for reasons "relating to security and the prevention of terrorism."

Security sources said Israel had feared the extradition would spark a wave of violence, adding to the clashes that have flared daily for two weeks in the West Bank since Israel broke ground for 6,500 homes for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem.

"My understanding is that everything is done," Abu Marzook said, referring to the apparent agreement that he would be deported to Jordan, the country that asked him to leave two years ago under pressure from Israel.
"I think they are going to do something before Monday," said Abu Marzook, who was relaxed and dressed in a prison-issue orange jumpsuit.
Asked whether he believed he would be freed from jail and sent to Jordan before a court hearing scheduled on Monday, he said: "Yes, this is my expectation."
In Washington, U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno told reporters the 47-year-old Palestinian political activist would remain in U.S. custody.
"It is in the INS (Immigration and Naturalisation Service) process, and we are reviewing all of our options." She said a "detainer" had been filed to keep him in a U.S. jail.

But Jordan's Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali told Reuters Television: "If the Americans are asking Jordan to let him go back to the area and be in Jordan, Jordan will look into it and try to help."
"If he wants, and the U.S. would like him to go there (Jordan), then we would look into it favourably." He said any decision would be taken on humanitarian grounds.

In the interview in a visiting room of the Manhattan Correctional Centre, Abu Marzook said that a Jordanian official had gone to his suburban family home in Virginia in recent days and told his wife that King Hussein was "doing his best" to arrange for his transfer to Jordan.

Israel alleged that the Palestinian was responsible as the head of Hamas's political wing for attacks that killed scores of Israelis in recent years, but did not contend that he personally committed any acts of violence.

Abu Marzook denied involvement in any violence but he opposes the 1993 accords signed by Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation leader Yasser Arafat, which created the self-ruled Palestinian Authority in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.

Abu Marzook, who had lived in the United States as an engineering student and businessman since 1982, said that if he returned to Jordan, "I will continue doing my job, to keep my commitment to serving my people. I think peace is a very beautiful word for everybody... but not the peace as Netanyahu has it."

The activist's attorney argued in court two days ago that federal law required the U.S. government to surrender him to Israel no later than March 28, but prosecutors said the deadline under a two-month limitation that began when Abu Marzook dropped his appeal was April 6.
